\chapter{Dog and Cat}
\label{ch:ar-dog-and-cat}
\hlchaptermodality{21}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a dog and a cat in Arabic.}

Say kalb beside Hebrew kelev, then qiṭṭ beside Latin cattus, flagging that the cat link is still debated.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ar{كلب}, \ar{قط}]{\ar{كلب}, \ar{قط} — a solid root, and the word that closes the loop}

\label{lesson:AR-C21-kalb-qitt}



\begin{quote}
Spanish has a genuine dog-word mystery, and German another by way of English. Arabic's dog-word has no such mystery — and its cat-word turns out to be a long-lost cousin of nearly every European cat-word there is.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{\ar{كلب}} (\emph{kalb}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{dog}\textquotedblright{}) traces to \textbf{Proto-Semitic} \emph{\textbf{*kalb-}} — the exact same root behind \textbf{Hebrew}'s own word for dog, \textbf{\he{כֶּלֶב}} (\emph{kelev}) (the name \textbf{Caleb} is traditionally connected to this same root, though some scholars instead derive it from \emph{kol-lev}, \textquotedblleft{}whole-hearted\textquotedblright{}). Unlike Spanish's \emph{perro} or the English word that replaced \textquotedblleft{}hound,\textquotedblright{} \emph{kalb} is a solid, well-attested, unmysterious Semitic root, shared across the whole Semitic family (Aramaic, Akkadian, and more).
\end{culture}

\begin{culture}
Here's how this whole arc most likely ties together: \textbf{\ar{قط}} (\emph{qiṭṭ}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{cat, tomcat}\textquotedblright{}) is not just a coincidence-sounding lookalike — it's widely \textbf{compared} to the exact same ancient \textbf{Afro-Asiatic} root behind Latin's \textbf{cattus} (alongside Nubian \emph{kadis}, mentioned back in the Spanish and Latin lessons). Be honest about the uncertainty here, though: linguists don't fully agree on the relationship. Some argue \emph{qiṭṭ} and \emph{cattus} both descend from a \textbf{shared} ancestor; others have proposed that \emph{kadis} (and even \emph{qiṭṭ} itself) could be a \textbf{later} borrowing \textbf{from} Arabic rather than an independent cousin, reversing the direction. What's not in serious dispute is that Arabic's word for \textquotedblleft{}cat\textquotedblright{} sits in the same tangled word-family as Spanish's \emph{gato}, French's \emph{chat}, Italian's \emph{gatto}, and German's \emph{Katze} — one root (or a tight cluster of related roots), spreading out in every direction from wherever cats were first domesticated, even if the exact family tree is still being worked out.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kalb\textquotedblright{} — dog, a solid Semitic root, cousin of Hebrew's kelev
  \item \textquotedblleft{}qiṭṭ\textquotedblright{} — cat, most likely a distant cousin of Latin's cattus and every European cat-word there is
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What root does \textbf{\ar{كلب}} trace to, and what's its Hebrew cousin? (\textbf{Proto-Semitic \emph{*kalb-}}; cousin of Hebrew \textbf{\he{כֶּלֶב}}, \emph{kelev}.) Is \textbf{\ar{قط}}'s relationship to Latin's \emph{cattus} fully settled? (\textbf{No} — widely compared, most likely from a shared Afro-Asiatic root, but linguists still debate the exact relationship and direction.) What does this most likely mean for Arabic's word for \textquotedblleft{}cat\textquotedblright{} compared to Spanish's \emph{gato}, French's \emph{chat}, and German's \emph{Katze}? (\textbf{They most likely belong to the same tangled ancient word family} — spreading in every direction from the region where cats were first domesticated.)
\end{tcolorbox}
